Kendala Critical Minerals Ltd., a new private company, was registered at the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) on Oct. 16, 2026.
Its sole shareholder is U.S.-based KazAmerican Critical Minerals, Inc., headquartered in New York. The new company’s share capital is $1,000, consisting of 10,000 ordinary shares worth $0.10 each.
According to the AIFC, Kendala Critical Minerals Ltd. plans to engage in geological exploration, extraction, downstream processing and wholesale trading of critical minerals, strategic metals and rare earth elements.
The company will also manage subsoil-use rights, conduct geological exploration, prepare feasibility studies for metallurgical operations and enter into physical supply agreements with industrial partners.
On its official website, KazAmerican Critical Minerals says it is developing integrated supply chains for battery metals (including nickel, cobalt and lithium) and rare earth elements from Kazakhstan to the U.S. and partner countries. The company is set to use the Middle Corridor for transport of raw and processed materials.
American projects in Kazakhstan
A geological exploration company called KAZ Critical Minerals is already operating in Kazakhstan. However, there is no evidence that the two companies are affiliated; their names are simply similar.
KAZ Critical Minerals is a portfolio company of U.S. investment firm Cove Capital, which has already been developing large-scale projects focused on rare earth elements and critical metals in Kazakhstan.
Its portfolio includes a tungsten project in the Karaganda region. A joint venture, Cove Kaz Capital Group, established by Cove Capital and Kazakhstan’s national company Tau-Ken Samruk, is developing a major tungsten project comprising the Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty deposits in the Shet district.
The project includes the construction of mines, a mining and processing complex, and a hydrometallurgical plant worth between $1.1 billion and $1.2 billion. The feasibility study is expected to be completed by the end of 2027, while mining is scheduled to begin in 2030. The project is expected to produce ammonium paratungstate, with copper, bismuth and molybdenum concentrates recovered as byproducts.
Cove Capital is also conducting exploration for rare and rare earth metals in the East Kazakhstan and Kostanay regions in partnership with Kazgeology.

articles.title: Vietnam’s Strategic Shift: From Raw Rare Earths Exporter to Domestic Refiner - elciudadano.com
articles.summary: Vietnam’s Strategic Shift: From Raw Rare Earths Exporter to Domestic Refiner  elciudadano.com
articles.full_text:
Original article: Vietnam y su plan para girar de exportador de tierras raras en bruto a refinador en suelo nacional
For years, Vietnam has navigated a challenging position in the geopolitics of critical minerals: it holds the second-largest rare earth reserves in the world but exports nearly all its crude ore, primarily to China. Now, Hanoi aims to change this narrative. The Ministry of Industry and Trade has finalized a draft decree that, if enacted, would prohibit the export of unprocessed rare earth ore and 16 other strategic minerals, requiring that any sale abroad meets strict deep processing thresholds in Vietnam. This draft, submitted to the Ministry of Justice for review on October 8, is not yet law. However, its existence signifies a seismic shift in Hanoi’s strategy: moving from a raw materials supplier to a significant player in the global value chain.
The Draft: 17 Minerals Under Lock
The document, titled “List of Strategic and Important Minerals Permitted for Export and their Processing Levels”, identifies 17 of the 19 minerals on Vietnam’s strategic list. It includes rare earths, tin, tungsten, antimony, copper, bauxite, titanium, lithium, iron, manganese, molybdenum, nickel, cobalt, chromite, anthracite coal, apatite, and graphite. Uranium, thorium, and gold are excluded from this specific regime.
The rule is simply formulated but radical in effect: only products that have reached the specified deep processing level for each mineral may be exported. Direct export of raw ore or concentrates is prohibited. For tin, for instance, refined metal is required, even in ingots. Tungsten must be processed into ammonium paratungstate (APT) or tungsten oxide. Copper is allowed only in refined cathodes or plates.
The case for rare earths is even more restrictive. They do not follow the general rule of the draft, which allows the export of any product that surpasses a processing threshold. Rare earths have a special management mechanism: they may only leave the country in one of five forms: individual rare earth oxides (separated), rare earth metals, alloys, alloy powders, or permanent magnets. Minerals, concentrates, and intermediate products are strictly prohibited.
No Transition, No New Procedures
Two details of the draft reveal the urgency with which Hanoi wants to implement this shift. First, there is no transition period. The criterion for determining if a shipment is governed by the new policy is the time of customs declaration. Contracts signed prior to the law’s enactment are not automatically protected. Second, the text does not create new administrative procedures, a concession to the exporting community that does not mitigate the impact of the fundamental prohibition.
The Gap Between Paper and Factory
According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), Vietnam possesses an estimated 22 million tons of rare earth oxides, roughly half of China’s reserves and more than any other country. Mining production has skyrocketed tenfold in recent years, increasing from 400 tons in 2021 to 4,300 tons by 2025, propelling Vietnam to the sixth-largest global producer, up from tenth place in 2021.
However, this explosive growth conceals a paradox that the draft seeks to rectify. Vietnam lacks a single operational industrial plant capable of refining ore into high-purity rare earth oxides (≥95%), the minimum standard for export and use in advanced technology. Current activities focus on extraction and primary processing. As Professor Tran Dai Lam from the Institute of Materials Science at the Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology states: “A country that possesses rare earths but only extracts and exports them as primary ore or concentrates is selling the lowest part of the value chain.”
The primary beneficiary of this dynamic has been China. Chinese customs data shows that imports of rare earth elements and concentrates from Vietnam doubled to nearly 12,000 tons in the last recorded year. Vietnam also imported rare earths to process and re-export, an anomaly the new framework seeks to eliminate.
The Legal Framework is Already in Progress
The Ministry of Industry and Trade’s draft is supported by a broader legislative change: the Amended Law on Geology and Minerals, approved by the National Assembly on December 11, 2025, and effective from January 1, 2026. This law formally classifies rare earths as a special strategic resource under strict state supervision and prohibits the export of raw ore. The regulation stipulates that only designated or authorized entities by the Government can carry out exploration, extraction, and processing activities for rare earths, with the State centrally managing geological data.
The Ministry of Industry’s draft operationalizes this legal prohibition, defining what is meant by “deep processing” for each mineral and closing the regulatory loophole that previously allowed the export of concentrates.
The Global Industry is Already Moving
Despite the draft not yet being enacted, the international private sector is already positioning itself. In March 2026, Australian Lynas Rare Earths—the largest rare earth producer outside of China—signed a framework agreement with South Korean LS Eco Energy to build a rare earth metal production facility in Vietnam. The facility will convert rare earth oxides into metals, initially prioritizing samarium, and produce neodymium-praseodymium metals (NdPr) and heavy elements like dysprosium and terbium, critical inputs for permanent magnets in electric vehicles and wind turbines. Both companies signed convertible instruments worth approximately 30 million Australian dollars each as a signal of long-term commitment.
Simultaneously, Hanoi has activated a regulatory sandbox mechanism to test semi-industrial-scale refining technology. In September 2026, the Hanoi People’s Committee authorized the Construction Consulting and Mining Technology Joint Stock Company to execute a pilot project to produce total rare earth oxides with purity above 95% from ore sourced from Dong Pao mine in Lai Chau province. The plant is designed for a capacity of 100 kilograms of ore per hour and a maximum of 100 tons of processed ore, with an 18-month testing period. The project is financed 80% by the company’s own resources.
The Challenge: Technology, Not Ore
Prime Minister Pham Minh Chinh himself has acknowledged that the central challenge is not a lack of resources but the absence of technological capacity to convert those resources into value. In a meeting of the Government’s Standing Committee in January 2026, Chinh emphasized the need to develop the rare earth industry to ensure national strategic autonomy, prioritizing deep processing, advanced technology transfer, public-private collaboration, and infrastructure development.
The official roadmap, however, is ambitious. The Government has planned to raise annual rare earth mineral production to 2 million tons by 2030, a goal that would multiply current production by more than 450 times. Achieving this would require not only massive investment in separation and refining plants but also the training of specialized human capital and resolution of regulatory bottlenecks that analysts believe still persist despite legislative advances.
What Is at Stake
If the draft is enacted without changes, Vietnam will cease to be a marginal supplier of concentrates and instead become a gatekeeper of its own subterranean resources. Countries that currently import Vietnamese raw ore—China primarily—will have to adapt: either purchase already processed products or establish refining capacity in Vietnam. For Western nations looking to diversify their rare earth supply chains away from China, Vietnam’s maneuver presents both an opportunity and a warning: Hanoi is not willing to be a mere raw material supplier in that strategy. It aims to be a partner and intends to retain the added value.
The draft is now in the hands of the Ministry of Justice. Its approval—or modification—will determine whether Vietnam successfully bridges the gap between the 22 million tons that lie beneath its soil and the magnets, alloys, and metals that the world requires.
The Citizen

articles.title: How Korea is deepening ties with Chile in critical minerals race - BNamericas
articles.summary: How Korea is deepening ties with Chile in critical minerals race  BNamericas
articles.full_text:
South Korea can stand out in the race for critical minerals in Chile by combining industrial demand, technology, and public-sector expertise, Wonseok Choi, Chief Representative Chile’s Office at the state-owned mining agency KOMIR, told BNamericas.
Given that the United States and the European Union are also taking steps to secure their supply chains, Choi proposed deepening ties between Chile and Korea gradually - starting with joint studies and demonstration projects - which could lead to significant corporate investments and off-take agreements.
BNamericas: How do you see KOMIR’s partnerships with Chilean mining companies and institutions developing under the Kast administration and Daniel Mas’s leadership at the economy and mining ministry?
Choi: I am optimistic. Cooperation between state-owned and private companies is a clear priority for this government. At Chile Day in London in September, Economy and Mining Minister Daniel Mas presented Codelco’s partnerships with global miners as a model in which state companies and private capital complement each other.
We can see this in recent projects. In August, Codelco and Pucobre formed a joint venture for the Tovaku copper project, and Enami is advancing Salares Altoandinos with Rio Tinto. State companies contribute mining rights, while private partners bring capital and development capabilities. Corfo and INLiSa [Instituto Nacional de Litio y Salares] are also widening cooperation on tailings and lithium technology.
I also see opportunities for Korea. In the exploration cooperation we are preparing with Enami, public institutions would carry out early surveys and assessments together, giving companies a basis to participate.
PRM, the precious metals recovery venture between LS MnM and Codelco, shows how Korean technology can be applied to local raw materials. Korean companies could expand their role by combining equity, long-term offtake, financing and processing technology to suit each project.
Such partnerships need trust if they are to last. Alongside changes to laws and procedures, permitting improvements should include early dialogue between regulators and companies to clarify requirements and discuss issues.
BNamericas: What led KOMIR to renew its memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Chilean state miner Enami in July, and what does each party gain?
Choi: The renewed MoU covers five years and includes joint efforts to identify promising exploration projects. It also expands our technical cooperation to include joint research and development on mineral processing, resource recovery from mining waste, mine rehabilitation and smelter modernization. Cooperation on exploration is our priority. Much of Chile’s mining investment goes into expanding existing mines, and competition for good assets remains strong. We need to consider early-stage projects as well when looking for future sources of supply.
For Enami, this cooperation offers opportunities to find partners for promising mining properties and improve technologies, such as more efficient copper recovery from slag. For KOMIR, it allows us to assess Chilean projects at an earlier stage and connect them with Korean companies. Since signing our MoU with Enami in 2022, we have already analyzed tailings samples, jointly visited lithium exploration sites, and organized events between Korean and Chilean companies to address investment matters.
BNamericas: How do you assess the five agreements signed by Chile and South Korea in July, which cover areas such as investment and trade, and, in particular, what priorities should be set for the mining sector?
Choi: President Lee Jae Myung’s visit in July broadened the relationship beyond trade into investment, security and Antarctic research. On mining, I would highlight the Mineral Resources Partnership MoU signed by Korea’s Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources and Chile’s Ministry of Mining. Building on the 2004 MoU, it extends cooperation across the value chain. This represents a step forward in cooperation with Chile, Korea’s first FTA partner.
The priorities should come from areas where the two countries’ strategies meet. Chile’s Critical Minerals Strategy aims to diversify production and add more value at home, and names Korea as a major trading partner. In September, Korea approved a plan to expand its critical minerals list to 51. It also plans to raise stockpiling targets to up to 365 days for minerals with vulnerable supply chains to strengthen supply resilience.
BNamericas: What specific areas of mining cooperation could the two countries move forward on?
Choi: I would suggest three areas for cooperation. First, we can jointly identify promising copper, lithium and rare earth projects and build long-term supply relationships. Stockpiling could be linked to this work where the minerals are on the stockpiling list and meet the relevant procurement requirements.
Second, we can extend cooperation along the value chain. Korea has globally competitive industries in smelting, battery materials, cell manufacturing and recycling, while Chile wants to add more value locally, including through stronger smelting and refining capacity. These strengths are complementary. We could work together to improve existing facilities through lower-carbon smelting and by-product recovery, or consider processing materials in Chile where it makes economic sense.
Third, we can cooperate on resource recovery, smart mining and mine environmental management, drawing on Korea’s public-sector experience in these areas. I think a step-by-step approach is realistic, starting with a few shared priorities for joint studies and demonstration projects. If the technology and economics are sound, this work can lead to corporate investment and offtake agreements.
BNamericas: Apart from Enami, which other mining companies in Chile have you signed collaboration agreements with this year?
Choi: The most important publicly announced agreement this year is our renewed MoU with Enami. We have also signed non-disclosure agreements with private lithium and rare earth companies in Chile, which allow us to examine technical information beyond what is public. We are currently reviewing data and visiting sites to assess opportunities for KOMIR and Korean companies to participate.
We also continue our institutional cooperation with Cochilco under the MoU signed in 2023. We are working on a project through Korea’s Knowledge Sharing Program (KSP) to help modernize Cochilco’s Chilean mining statistics and data.
BNamericas: How interested are Korean investors in developing lithium projects in Chile, and what is your outlook for progress on the National Lithium Strategy under the Kast administration?
Choi: Interest is very strong. Chile accounts for the vast majority of Korea’s lithium carbonate imports, and Korean battery manufacturers and automakers have signed long-term supply agreements with SQM. POSCO and LG Energy Solution were both shortlisted for Enami’s Salares Altoandinos partnership. Rio Tinto was ultimately selected as the development partner. Even so, Chile remains a priority for Korean companies because of its resources, accessibility and infrastructure.
The message of the National Lithium Strategy is clear. Development should use technologies such as direct lithium extraction (DLE) to reduce environmental impacts. It should also protect salt-flat ecosystems and bring benefits to local communities. The Kast government has taken a more investment-friendly approach, but the basic model of state participation in strategic salt flats remains in place.
There have also been concrete steps. The Codelco-SQM joint venture, Novandino Litio, was established at the end of last year to continue the Atacama operation. In August, Quiborax was awarded the first special lithium operating contract [CEOL], signed by the state exclusively with a private company, to recover lithium from residues left by boron processing. I see this as a positive sign that there is room for new approaches and participants.
Looking ahead, commercial production still comes only from the Salar de Atacama, so I hope there will be more ways for foreign companies and institutions to participate, with clearer conditions and procedures.
BNamericas: South Korea is looking to deepen its mining ties with Chile at a time when the United States and the European Union are also racing to secure their critical mineral supply chains. In that competitive landscape, what sets the Chile-Korea relationship apart?
Choi: Korea’s strength is the ability to bring together industrial demand, technology and public-sector experience. First, Korea can connect mineral resources with industrial demand. Our substantial demand and technologies in batteries, materials, smelting and recycling can support more value-added activity in Chile where the economics are sound. PRM, the JV between LS MnM and Codelco that recovers precious metals from copper refining by-products in Chile, is one example.
Second, public-sector cooperation can extend across the mine life cycle. KOMIR’s responsibilities combine support for resource development, mine rehabilitation and the revitalization of former mining regions. This gives us experience relevant to Chile’s priorities in tailings, water and mine closure. Third, trust. The Korea-Chile FTA was Korea’s first and Chile’s first with an Asian country, and bilateral trade has grown about fourfold since it took effect. As Chile diversifies its markets and partners, Korea is a natural long-term option.
While Korea has less experience in overseas mine operations than some established mining countries, its strength lies in combining public-sector support, industrial demand and technology. That is why I favor a phased approach: public institutions can reduce early uncertainty through surveys, technical reviews and information, while companies decide whether to participate on commercial grounds.

 IIT (ISM) Dhanbad’s 
Durga Puja pandal
 has combined tradition and scientific innovation to highlight critical minerals and semiconductor technology powering electronics, clean-energy systems, electric vehicles and India’s technological ambitions.
Built around the messages “Smaller Chips, Bigger Tomorrows” and “Critical Minerals for a Cleaner, Greener Future”, the pandal features illuminated crystal formations symbolising lithium, cobalt, nickel, copper and rare-earth elements. Semiconductor-inspired circuits and chip designs explain technologies behind everyday devices and sustainable development.
The theme highlights the institute’s critical-mineral research and semiconductor development. Its Centre of Excellence for Critical Minerals (CoRE-MiN), recognised under National Critical Mineral Mission in Aug 2025, was inaugurated by Union minister of coal and mines G. Kishan Reddy on Dec 23-2025.
IIT (ISM) also hosts a satellite campus of India–UK Critical Minerals Global Supply Chain Observatory with TEXMiN and University of Cambridge’s Institute for Manufacturing to study global mineral supply chains. An indigenous semiconductor chip developed by an IIT (ISM) team was recently presented to Prime Minister 
Narendra Modi
.
Director Sukumar Mishra, chief patron of the organising committee for Durga Puja, Lakshmi Puja and Kali Puja 2026, said the theme linked cultural traditions with technologies crucial to India’s progress and sustainable development.
Dean (faculty) and committee president M.K. Singh said the initiative promoted awareness of science, research and innovation. Registrar Prabodh Pandey said the celebration strengthened campus unity and added an educational dimension.
The community Durga Puja began in 1977 during then-director G.S. Marwah’s tenure and has since united faculty, employees, students and their families.

articles.title: Daily on Energy: FERC moves to accelerate LNG projects - Washington Examiner
articles.summary: Daily on Energy: FERC moves to accelerate LNG projects  Washington Examiner
articles.full_text:
WHAT’S HAPPENING TODAY: Good afternoon and happy Thursday, readers! Several major new movies are hitting the theaters this weekend: Sense and Sensibility for the romantics, Whalefall for the thrill seekers, and Nathan Fielder’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, You Can See Everything, for everyone else who’s chronically online. Which one will you be seeing?
- But first, today’s edition of Daily on Energy takes a look at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s latest move to speed up approvals for liquefied natural gas projects.
Welcome to Daily on Energy, written by Washington Examiner energy and environment writers Callie Patteson (@CalliePatteson) and Maydeen Merino (@MaydeenMerino). Email cpatteson@washingtonexaminer dot com or mmerino@washingtonexaminer dot com for tips, suggestions, calendar items, and anything else. If a friend sent this to you and you’d like to sign up, click here. If signing up doesn’t work, shoot us an email, and we’ll add you to our list.
FASTER APPROVALS AND FEW ENVIRONMENTAL HURDLES FOR LNG:
Federal energy regulators are making it easier to develop liquefied natural gas infrastructure across the country, proposing a new blanket authorization program and removing certain environmental requirements for new projects.
Earlier today, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission put forward the new policies, which will help deliver on President Donald Trump’s agenda to develop more natural gas projects and increase exports of LNG abroad.
Blanket authorizations: The regulators unanimously proposed establishing a blanket program to authorize certain activities at LNG facilities. This will allow some projects to move forward at an accelerated pace without undergoing a case-by-case authorization process that can take months or even years.
FERC is breaking up this blanket program into three tiers, meaning not all projects will be eligible to move forward without any federal review.
The first tier is “automatic authorization,” allowing projects to proceed without advanced notice to the commission. Eligible projects must not increase an LNG plant’s authorization capacity, cannot expand authorized vertical or horizontal extension within the facility’s footprint, and cannot exceed design limits for flows, volumes, pressures, temperatures, and more.
This second tier requires developers to provide a 60-day notice to the commission and provide an opportunity for the agency and stakeholders to protest against the action.
Projects eligible for this tier are similar to those in the first; however, it also encompasses some projects that may increase the capacity of an LNG facility. Those activities must also be located within the LNG plant footprint, must not cause a significant adverse impact to reliability, risks, or public safety, and cannot cause any changes outside design limits of new and existing equipment.
The third and final tier requires developers to provide a 90-day notice to the commission before moving forward and provide a protest period for staff and stakeholders. Projects that fall under this tier specifically involve the construction of new LNG infrastructure, including liquefaction trains, tanks, and marine berths.
Softening environmental reviews: FERC is also aiming to speed up the development of LNG projects by reducing federal permitting requirements.
Specifically, the agency is softening environmental reviews required under the National Environmental Policy Act. The regulators proposed to no longer request air dispersion modeling from applicants or rely on the modeling when assessing operating air quality effects under NEPA.
The commission did not unanimously agree to this proposal, with Democratic commissioner Judy Chang dissenting.
Chang said she is concerned that softening the requirements will leave FERC “without adequate information to meet its obligations under NEPA and the Natural Gas Act,” saying the air dispersion modeling is the “best tool” the agency has for understanding local and regional air impacts of projects.
FERC Chair Laura Swett defended the proposed rule after the agency’s open meeting today, telling reporters it is “not a short cut” putting the environment and communities at risk.
“This is simply a statement that we are, in my words, an economic regulator, not an environmental regulator, and we certainly are not an air expert, whereas other agencies on the federal level and the state level are,” Swett said.
Read more from Callie here.
All the rest:
IEA TO RELEASE MORE THAN 400 MILLION BARRELS OF OIL: The International Energy Agency plans to release more than 400 million barrels of oil that was initially agreed upon in March.
The IEA met today to discuss the scale and timing for releasing emergency reserves.The group said it would complete the release of the remaining 100 million barrels of oil it approved in March. It noted that the total would exceed 400 million barrels because some members have released more than initially agreed to.
So far, the IEA said it has released 330 million barrels from emergency stock. Members have also agreed to expedite the release of the remaining volumes, which will also include more than 20 million barrels of diesel.
However, Bloomberg reported that the U.S. was unhappy with the IEA’s current plan to release oil stock, arguing that it does not go far enough to stop rising fuel prices.
It noted that U.S. officials were advocating for the group to release at least an additional 100 million barrels of oil, but did not formally make the proposal at today’s meeting.
Read more by Maydeen here.
VENTURE GLOBAL LOOKS TO POWER AI: LNG giant Venture Global is getting in on the race to power artificial intelligence, signing deals with GE Vernova and Baker Hughes this week.
The agreements, announced this morning, are expected to support the development of 16 new power generation units as well as additional off-grid resources, according to Reuters.
The initial “power-island” units will generate up to 720 megawatts of power each. They reportedly could also support up to 10 gigawatts of compute capacity by the end of 2034, Venture Global said.
These units would be gas-fired and combined-cycle, and would not pull from any public electricity grid or water utilities – operating behind-the-meter.
Venture Global plans to file its first permit applications this week and intends on ordering its first unit by the end of the year, according to Reuters.
SENATE DEMOCRATS PRESSES EPA TO DROP ABORTION PILL WATER QUALITY STUDY: Senate Democrats are urging the Environmental Protection Agency to drop its study assessing the presence of abortion pill chemicals in the water.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and Democratic Sen. Patty Murray of Washington along with 45 other Democrats sent a letter to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, urging him to remove the abortion pills mifepristone and misoprostol from the list of medications that the agency monitors in drinking water.
The senators argued that the agency’s inclusion of mifepristone and misoprostol in the study is part of a “radical, anti-science campaign” from anti-abortion advocates seeking to restrict access to abortion drugs.
Some background: The EPA in September announced that mifepristone and misoprostol would be included among a list of more than 1,400 other chemicals as part of a new water quality Non-Targeted Analysis study, an assessment method that can identify thousands of possible pollutants at a time.
Read more by Washington Examiner’s healthcare reporter Gabrielle Etzel here.
NUCLEAR REGULATORS APPROVE PLAN TO REMOVE DAMAGED FUEL RODS DELAYING PALISADES RESTART: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has given Holtec International the greenlight to remove a damaged nuclear fuel assembly in its Palisades Nuclear Power Plant using a method never used before.
If you forgot: Holtec is restarting the Palisades Nuclear Power Plant in western Michigan, which has been closed since 2022. Shortly after Holtec started to load the nuclear fuel at the end of August, one nuclear fuel assembly – a group of fuel rods – tilted and tipped out of place.
The incident damaged the assembly’s “upper tie plate,” which caps and secures the fuel rods. As a result, workers were not able to use traditional retrieval methods to remove the damaged assembly.
The unusual fix: Holtec then asked federal regulators for an emergency approval, amending its license to allow the company to use special equipment to remove the assembly from the reactor cavity and to the facility’s spent fuel pool.
The “first of a kind” process involves lifting the fuel assembly out of the water located in the reactor, which helps provide shielding from radiation and contain radioactive material from damaged fuel rods.
The NRC approved the method this week, saying it is required to resume fuel loading activities.
Holtec officials have insisted that the fuel rods within the assembly were not damaged in the incident.
KEN PAXTON TARGETS DATA CENTERS OVER WATER USE: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sent a letter to 156 data center developments across the state, requesting information on water usage.
Paxton, the Republican nominee in the Texas Senate race, said the requests are part of an investigation launched last month into hundreds of data center developments.
He said some of those projects have yet to respond to a water use survey from the Texas Water Development Board.
“Data center developers must follow the law and respect the Texans and communities affected by their operations,” Paxton said in a news release. “I am actively investigating data centers across Texas to make sure that Texans and our natural resources are protected.”
SENATE MIDTERM CANDIDATES ON CLIMATE AND ENERGY: Democrats on the campaign trail have placed a greater focus on energy costs as a central issue amongst voters.
At the same time, they have shifted away from climate messaging. In 2019, many Democrats championed federal climate initiatives like the “Green New Deal.”

SINGAPORE – In March 2022, as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine accelerated a global energy crisis, Singapore subtly signalled its changed stance on nuclear energy.
A report commissioned by the Energy Market Authority on the Republic’s energy future had put nuclear power back on the table, projecting it could meet up to 10 per cent of the country’s electricity needs by 2050.
In a geopolitically fragmented world where the land-constrained Republic has limited options to cut emissions, the report highlighted the promise of advanced nuclear technologies such as small modular reactors (SMRs) in helping to power the country.
SMRs are compact nuclear reactors that can be factory-assembled and installed closer to urban areas due to their smaller footprint.
This came a decade after Singapore in 2012 ruled out the use of conventional nuclear plants, due to their risks for the small and dense city-state. But Singapore had at that time kept the door open for future nuclear energy technologies.
Four years after the report was published, the Republic is thoroughly examining a nuclear future for itself – not just to meet its climate commitments, but also to safeguard its energy security.
Singapore now relies on burning natural gas, the cleanest of planet-warming fossil fuels, for about 95% of its energy needs.
But South-east Asia is grappling with the worst energy crisis since the 1970s, this time due to a war waged by Israel and the US on Iran.
Iran responded to the attacks by blockading the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway through which supplies of oil and gas are shipped from the Middle East to the rest of the world.
About 20% of the South-east Asian region’s liquefied natural gas imports in 2025 transited through this maritime choke point, with Singapore accounting for over half of these volumes, according to an International Energy Agency report published in October.
Energy analysts, observers and researchers told The Straits Times that geopolitical instability, the global agenda to decarbonise, and advancements in nuclear technology have helped revive the region’s ambitions to tap the energy source.
ASEAN countries including Vietnam, Thailand and the Philippines are taking steps to incorporate nuclear energy into their fuel mix.
Nuclear security researcher Julius Cesar Imperial Trajano attributed the growing interest of ASEAN countries in nuclear energy to the converging pressures of safeguarding energy security, rising electricity demand from energy-intensive industries and data centres, and shifting away from planet-warming fossil fuels.
“Nuclear is increasingly being considered not simply as a climate solution but also as a potential source of reliable, low-carbon electricity that can complement renewables,” said the research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS).
While the Singapore Government has not made a decision on nuclear energy, it has beefed up its capacity to study the energy source, while announcing its plan to undergo a readiness assessment by the UN atomic watchdog in 2027.
It has also signed at least seven pacts with countries and firms within the nuclear energy ecosystem over the past two years.
A secure energy future
Experts point to the variety of uranium fuel sources and the ability of countries to stockpile it as being among the ways that nuclear reactors can contribute to energy security.
In April, Minister-in-charge of Energy and Science and Technology in the Ministry of Trade and Industry Tan See Leng told Parliament that five one-inch-tall uranium pellets can generate the same amount of electricity as one Olympic-sized swimming pool of natural gas.
A spokesman for the World Nuclear Association (WNA), an international organisation representing the civil nuclear industry, told ST: “Uranium is sourced from a range of geopolitically diverse countries, and nuclear fuel is extremely energy dense, so many years worth of fuel can be stored on site – insulating countries from the supply and price shocks seen in oil and gas markets.”
Today’s supply shocks are having an effect similar to that of the oil crises of the 1970s, which had prompted countries such as France, Sweden and Japan to embark on major nuclear build programmes, he added.
He said: “Moving away from imported fossil fuels will strengthen energy security across the region.”
David Broadstock of the Asia-Pacific energy industry consultancy Lantau Group said the war in the Middle East is but the latest in a string of energy crises that Singapore has endured since around 2020.
Reducing the impact of such events on energy bills will require a changed energy mix, he added.
“Nuclear becomes an attractive solution here in many ways, since it can produce large volumes of electricity with stable cost profiles,” Broadstock added.
The cost of imported natural gas and power generation makes up more than 75% of the regulated electricity tariff. This means that fluctuations in fuel costs due to geopolitical developments can impact the price consumers pay.
Meanwhile, stockpiled nuclear fuel will be able to produce electricity at a predictable cost.
Across ASEAN, member states have already moved to translate nuclear plans into policy.
Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand now have numerical estimates for nuclear capacity in their national plans, according to the 9th ASEAN Energy Outlook report published in October.
These range from a capacity of 600 megawatts for Thailand by 2050, to Indonesia’s goal of relying on nuclear energy for 12.1 per cent of its electricity mix by 2060.
Malaysia also formalised the integration of nuclear energy into its future energy mix in 2025, although no target figure was cited.
Ming Tan, global practice lead for nuclear energy at engineering consultancy Mott MacDonald, said a regional approach to nuclear power could benefit countries, allowing them to share knowledge, adopt common safety and technical principles, as well as reduce unnecessary duplication of effort.
“This can make it easier for countries to build capability, develop regulatory frameworks and learn from each other’s experiences while fully retaining national decision-making authority.”
A long-term domestic source of energy generation is especially pertinent for ASEAN nations, he said, as the region relies heavily on imported fuels shipped through some of the world’s busiest shipping routes.
The British-based firm was appointed by the Singapore Government in 2025 to study the safety and feasibility of advanced nuclear technologies like SMRs.
The promise of the small modular reactor
The global pivot towards nuclear power is in part powered by the rise of advanced reactors, which promise enhanced safety features and less radioactive waste, according to analysts.
According to the Nuclear Energy Agency, an intergovernmental agency that facilitates cooperation among countries with advanced nuclear technology, the number of SMR designs around the world has grown from 98 in 2024 to 156 in its latest assessment published in September.
Over the past five years, discussions about SMRs have moved beyond purely conceptual designs, said RSIS’ Trajano.
He cited developments such as greater regulatory engagement, progress towards licensing in some jurisdictions, and more attention to factory fabrication.
In September, for instance, the US’ Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved a construction permit for its first SMR after a 14-month review.
Analysts and observers said SMRs could require significantly smaller safety restriction zones than conventional nuclear reactors. This gives it an advantage over conventional reactors, especially for Singapore, other small island states and densely populated areas.
Conventional reactors typically require safety zones to be established within a 15km to 30km radius from the nuclear plant. In 2008, Singapore revealed it had considered reclaiming land at Pedra Branca to satisfy this buffer. However, the plan was dropped, as the island is less than 30km away from neighbouring Malaysia.
A spokesman for the NUS Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute (SNRSI) said smaller reactor fuel inventories and enhanced safety features in SMRs could reduce the potential consequences of severe accidents and, subject to safety assessments and regulatory requirements, could allow for smaller emergency planning zones.
He added: “Newer reactor designs increasingly incorporate natural circulation, gravity and other passive safety systems to maintain cooling, reducing reliance on external power and operator intervention.”
The nuclear incident in Fukushima in 2011 occurred because a power loss had cut off cooling to reactors there, causing them to overheat and melt down.
The SNRSI spokesman cited the tri-structural isotropic fuel used in high-temperature gas-cooled reactors, a kind of SMR. Such fuels can improve the containment of radioactive materials by coating uranium kernels in layers of ceramic and carbon, reducing the risk of a meltdown.
The WNA spokesman said that the modular format of SMRs is also an advantage, as they are easier to manufacture repeatedly in factories, instead of needing to build each one from scratch.
He said: “Many of the SMR designs proposed for near-term deployment are not technological leaps; rather, they offer a potential step change in how nuclear is delivered, through factory-based, repeatable manufacturing and deployment.”
The geopolitics of SMR development
Despite the promise of SMRs, most designs remain at an early stage of commercial deployment, said Nick Ash, energy advisory leader at engineering consultancy Arup, which is advising the UK’s SMR programme.
According to the Nuclear Energy Agency’s latest assessment, only Russia and China operate commercial SMRs.
Uncertainty remains over whether their projected cost and delivery advantages will be demonstrated once financing, supporting infrastructure, fuel supply and waste management are taken into account, Ash added.

articles.title: Lithium’s New Supply Chain: What EnergyX’s $2bn Deal Tells Manufacturers - IOL
articles.summary: Lithium’s New Supply Chain: What EnergyX’s $2bn Deal Tells Manufacturers  IOL
articles.full_text:
EnergyX’s ten-year, $2 billion take-or-pay agreement to supply Trafigura with 100,000 tonnes of lithium from Chile and the United States matters less for its size than for what it signals. A commodities trader is backing direct lithium extraction (DLE), a technology still proving itself commercially, and the demand behind it is increasingly stationary storage rather than electric vehicles. Take-or-pay terms oblige the buyer to pay whether or not it collects the metal. That gives developers the revenue certainty lenders want, which is why the deal also supports EnergyX’s export-credit application.
Storage is the new anchor
For years, EVs set lithium’s cycle. Now grid batteries are offsetting uneven vehicle sales. Orient Securities projects 2026 storage demand of roughly 570,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, about 55% higher year on year. Chemistry magnifies the effect: lithium iron phosphate (LFP) typically needs 30–50% more lithium per kWh than nickel-rich systems, because lower energy density means more cells for the same duty. Prices reflect the tightening. Fastmarkets expects an average of about $23,800 per tonne in 2026, above the roughly $20,000 that underpins the EnergyX contract. For manufacturers, demand driven by multi-year utility projects is steadier than consumer sentiment, but cheap lithium can no longer be assumed.
DLE: option value, not baseline supply
DLE draws lithium from brine using filters or sorbents instead of evaporation ponds, promising faster, smaller-footprint production. Industry reporting describes it entering commercial-scale production, and Benchmark has estimated it could supply a meaningful share of global output by the early 2030s if the project pipeline delivers on schedule. Delivery risk is real. EnergyX does not plan production until 2028 in Chile and 2029 in Texas, still needs funding for both plants, and awaits a decision on a $690 million Export-Import Bank loan. Its system combines known filtration technologies using readily available equipment, which eases engineering risk, but performance at commercial scale remains unproven. Peers are similarly early: LibertyStream aims to commission its first commercial-scale plant by the end of December 2026, while Empower EIT is targeting first commercial sales in 2027. Buyers should treat DLE volumes as valuable optionality before 2028, not dependable base supply.
The bottleneck is moving downstream
Lithium chemicals are only one constraint. The US is rebuilding storage-cell manufacturing, with LG Energy Solution and Samsung converting EV lines to LFP. LG aims to exceed 50 GWh of LFP storage capacity across five North American sites by the end of 2026, yet China still supplied 66.5% of US battery imports in the second quarter, down from 77% a year earlier. Tariffs on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries were due to rise from 7.5% to 25% in January 2026, but Benchmark forecasts US demand for LFP storage cells will outstrip North American production until 2028. There is an irony in the EnergyX deal: Trafigura intends to sell initially to Chinese customers, because that is where processing and cell capacity sits. Western lithium will not become western batteries automatically.
Practical implications
Manufacturers can draw four lessons.
- Contract in layers. Combine conventional supply with DLE-backed offtakes, and scrutinise pricing mechanisms. EnergyX’s deal is tied to prices near today’s levels, so fixed and floating exposure both carry risk.
- Keep chemistry flexibility. Trafigura will take 5,000 tonnes a year each of hydroxide and carbonate, reflecting that cell makers favour one or the other by application. Qualifying both reduces switching costs.
- Back suppliers early. General Motors’ and Eni’s stakes in EnergyX show carmakers and energy groups securing upstream positions before capacity exists.
- Budget for transition costs. Domestic content and supply diversification will likely carry a premium until scale arrives.
The deal shows lithium supply being re-engineered around storage demand, new extraction methods and shifting trade rules. For manufacturers, resilience will come from contracts, qualification and partnerships made now, long before the first DLE tonne ships.

Reviewed by Tom Sullivan
First reported on MINING.com
30 Second Briefing
Projected mine and processing capacity will cover only 68% of lithium demand, 74% of cobalt and 75% of copper by 2035, with GEM Mining Consulting’s new Volume Scarcity Index scoring lithium at 80/100 for tightness. GEM’s parallel Supply Chain Fragility Index rates rare earth magnets at 95/100 and battery-grade graphite at 89/100 because refining and magnet production are heavily concentrated in China, with diversified rare earth magnet capacity outside China meeting just 15% of global demand. The firm estimates a nominal 100,000 t/y project typically yields only about 60,200 t/y of reliable, qualified output once permitting delays, ramp-up losses, metallurgical recoveries and customer specifications are factored in.
Technical Brief
- GEM’s “reserve relevance” chain requires deposits to be financed, permitted, extracted, processed, qualified and delivered.
- Supply Chain Fragility Index incorporates processing concentration, technological dependence and geographic risk into a single score.
- Nickel’s fragility score of 66 is linked to processing concentration in Indonesia and China.
- Copper’s relatively low fragility score of 36 contrasts with its projected physical supply deficit.
- GEM’s 100,000 t/y nameplate example falls to 60,200 t/y after cumulative development and operating losses.
- Loss drivers include permitting/financing delays, slow ramp-up to nameplate and sub‑100% metallurgical recoveries.
- Additional derating occurs where plant output fails to meet tight chemical/technical specifications of battery and magnet customers.
- GEM argues smaller deposits with proven processing routes and offtake can be strategically superior to larger, unqualified resources.
Our Take
The same GEM Mining Consulting work cited here underpins the 11 August 2026 brief in our database, which stresses that the 68–75% lithium, cobalt and copper coverage to 2035 is after factoring in typical project slippage, so planners should treat these gaps as post-risk, not optimistic, numbers.
With rare earth magnets showing 107% notional 2035 coverage but a 95/100 fragility score and only 15% diversified supply outside China, OEMs in Europe and the USA are likely to prioritise localisation of magnet manufacturing rather than raw ore projects alone.
The 20%-plus gold price drop since the start of the US–Iran war, combined with copper’s 62/100 scarcity index, reinforces a pattern in our coverage where gold-heavy portfolios are underperforming relative to copper- and battery-metal-focused miners in capital-allocation discussions.

The US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) has proposed a program to speed up approval of expansions at US liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminals. As The Hill reports, the commission proposes limiting the deadlines for notices and objections regarding such applications to 60 or 90 days.
Regulator’s arguments
FERC Chair Laura Swett said the changes would allow the country to expand the capacity of existing facilities more quickly in order to supply gas to allies that urgently need it. According to her, the proposed procedure is also intended to preserve safety and environmental protection requirements.
The commission also proposes eliminating the requirement for planned gas projects to submit certain air pollution data during environmental reviews. Specifically, this concerns air pollutant dispersion models that simulate the interaction of a project’s emissions with other atmospheric pollutants to assess the impact on air quality.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Environmentalists’ objections
Swett called such models a source of confusion, delays and litigation risks. At the same time, FERC Commissioner Judy Chang disagreed with this assessment: in her view, modeling is the best tool for understanding projects’ likely local and regional effects on air quality.
Environmental organizations criticized both proposals. Claire Dorner of the Sierra Club said that accelerating LNG infrastructure development and easing modeling requirements would make it more difficult to assess the impact of gas projects on air quality in communities. She also argues that relaxing these rules could worsen conditions for local ecosystems and communities and intensify the climate crisis.

articles.title: U.S. Crude Inventories Plunge 8.6 Million Barrels, WTI Surges 3% Back Above $98 - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: U.S. Crude Inventories Plunge 8.6 Million Barrels, WTI Surges 3% Back Above $98  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
International oil prices diverged on Thursday (Oct. 15), with U.S. crude inventories falling far more than market expectations, driving New York West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures up more than 3% to reclaim the $98-per-barrel level. London Brent crude, meanwhile, settled slightly lower as investors weighed signals that the United States may ease sanctions on the shadow fleet. Geopolitical risks in the Middle East continued to escalate, with frequent attacks around the Strait of Hormuz keeping risk premiums elevated.
Data released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) showed that for the week ended Oct. 9, U.S. crude inventories plunged by 8.6 million barrels to 415.6 million barrels. The drawdown was far steeper than the market consensus estimate of a 288,000-barrel decline, serving as the primary catalyst behind the WTI rally. Distillate inventories also declined, while gasoline stockpiles bucked the trend and increased.
Behind the sharp inventory drawdown was hurricane-induced supply disruption. Hurricane Isaias swept through the Gulf of Mexico last week, prompting U.S. offshore producers to evacuate more than 130 platforms and rigs, temporarily shutting in roughly 1.5 million barrels per day of crude production—equivalent to about 70% of Gulf of Mexico offshore output. The hurricane made landfall near Destin, Florida, on the evening of Oct. 9.
WTI futures for November delivery settled up $2.88, or 3.03%, at $97.97 per barrel (approximately NT$3,200). Brent crude for December delivery settled down 14 cents, or 0.13%, at $105.92 per barrel (approximately NT$3,400).
U.S. Weighs Easing Shadow Fleet Restrictions
Another market focal point is the potential shift in U.S. government policy toward sanctions on the "shadow fleet." The term refers to a network of vessels that have long been covertly transporting oil for sanctioned countries such as Russia, Iran, and Venezuela. Sources indicated that Washington is discussing allowing "legitimate oil" to be transported via previously sanctioned vessels, in an effort to alleviate pressure from soaring global tanker freight rates.
The timing of these discussions comes just days after U.S. President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel—a decision that has already drawn backlash from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, European allies, and some Republican senators.
The U.S. Department of Energy emphasized that even if sanctions on the shadow fleet are eased, it would not make it easier for Russia to transport oil or petroleum products. The Treasury Department deferred related questions to the Energy Department. Market interpretation suggests the primary objective of the new proposal is to accelerate the flow of crude and refined products from the Persian Gulf region, rather than to greenlight Russian or Iranian oil exports.
However, market research firm Energy Aspects remains skeptical about the actual impact. The firm noted that shadow fleet vessels are generally old and poorly maintained, making it difficult for them to return to mainstream commercial fleets in large numbers in the short term. Moreover, most tankers sanctioned for their ties to Russia or Venezuela have continued operating over the past three months. Insurance requirements pose another hurdle—even if Washington eases sanctions, vessel insurers must still comply with EU and UK regulations, meaning at best only a handful of ships could be deployed for short-haul shuttle transport in the Strait of Hormuz.
Middle East Conflict Fuels Risk Premium
Geopolitics continues to weigh heavily on oil markets. Over the past 10 days, attacks on vessels in waters surrounding the Strait of Hormuz have increased significantly, with Iran leading the escalation—Tehran has stated it is intensifying attacks in response to the U.S. blockade of its ports and the stricter sanctions imposed last month. Meanwhile, attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia have also escalated markedly, creating two interconnected fronts. Any escalation in tensions along the world's most critical oil transit chokepoint will continue to provide support for oil prices on supply-disruption concerns.

IEA Launches Diesel Reserve Release
Against the backdrop of persistently high refined product prices, the International Energy Agency (IEA) announced Thursday that member countries have agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves "as soon as possible." The move aims to ease pressure from surging global fuel prices, though the IEA did not provide a specific timeline for the release in its statement.
In terms of volume, 20 million barrels of diesel is roughly equivalent to less than one day of global diesel demand, or slightly more than five days of U.S. diesel consumption. The Group of Seven (G7) had previously stated on Oct. 2 that it would release substantial volumes of diesel to the market within 20 days. This diesel is not a new release program but rather the remaining portion of a collective action initiated in March—when all 32 IEA member countries unanimously agreed to release a record 400 million barrels, of which approximately 330 million barrels have already been deployed to the market. If the IEA follows the same timeframe, member countries would need to release at a pace of roughly 1 million barrels per day for nearly three weeks.
The Paris-based IEA has more than 30 member countries, encompassing the United States and major allies across Europe and Asia. Market participants believe this coordinated action signals that major consuming nations' tolerance for current oil price levels is declining, which could exert some downward pressure on refined product prices in the short term, though the actual impact will depend on the pace of releases and developments in the Middle East.
Japan's Predicament: Over 90% of Crude Passes Through This Chokepoint
The crisis has hit Japan more directly than other major economies. Japan relies on Middle Eastern crude for more than 90% of its needs, and according to statistics from the Agency for Natural Resources and Energy under the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, Japan held petroleum reserves (including national and private) of approximately 72.89 million kiloliters as of the end of January this year—equivalent to 248 days, or roughly eight months of consumption.
With the Strait of Hormuz effectively blockaded since March, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry decided on March 24, under the Oil Stockpiling Act, to release approximately 8.5 million kiloliters from national reserves, valued at approximately ¥540 billion (approximately $3.4 billion). Shipments began on March 26 from five national reserve bases—Tomakomai East, Kikuma, Shirashima, Kamigoto, and Shibushi—marking only the second time the national reserve system has been tapped since the law was enacted in 1975 and the reserve program launched in 1978. At the same time, the private reserve requirement was reduced by 15 days.
Japan's hoped-for alternative route has also been disrupted: Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, which runs from eastern oil fields to the Red Sea coast, was halted by a drone attack in September. The roughly 1,200-kilometer pipeline is a critical artery for bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Ryosei Akazawa said in September that no additional reserve releases would be necessary in October, and that decisions from November onward would depend on Saudi Arabia's repair progress.
The following table summarizes the reserve releases by major economies during this cycle:
| Date | Entity | Action | Scale | 
|---|---|---|---|
| March 2026 | IEA 32 member countries | Record coordinated release | 400 million barrels | 
| March 24, 2026 | Japan | National crude reserve release | ~8.5 million kiloliters | 
| Oct. 2, 2026 | G7 | Coordinated release over 4 months | 100 million barrels, with substantial diesel in first 20 days | 
| Oct. 15, 2026 | IEA | Accelerated release of remaining allocation | Over 20 million barrels of diesel | 
Overall, the crude market is locked in a tug-of-war between bullish and bearish forces: sharply lower U.S. inventories and Middle East risk premiums provide downside support for prices, while the potential easing of shadow fleet sanctions and IEA strategic reserve releases create overhead pressure. Investors will be closely watching developments in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as the trajectory of U.S. sanctions policy toward Russia and Iran.

articles.title: Brazil's Eneva plans to invest US$80mn in LNG terminal to supply thermal plants in Ceará - BNamericas
articles.summary: Brazil's Eneva plans to invest US$80mn in LNG terminal to supply thermal plants in Ceará  BNamericas
articles.full_text:
Brazil's Eneva plans to invest around 400 million reais (US$80mn) in the construction of a liquefied natural gas (LNG) regasification terminal at the Port of Pecém, in the state of Ceará, to supply three gas-fired thermal power plants that won the backup capacity auction (LRCAP) held in March.
The investment is included in the physical–financial schedule submitted to the National Agency of Petroleum, Natural Gas and Biofuels (ANP) by Jandaia Geração de Energia, the subsidiary that submitted the request for authorization to build the project.
To serve the power plants, the project calls for the installation of a floating storage and regasification unit for LNG (FSRU, in its English acronym), with capacity to store 146.000m³ of liquefied gas and regasify up to 14 million m³/d of natural gas.
Read also: How two winners of Brazil’s largest power auction are ensuring the schedule
The unit will remain permanently moored at a new pier, called Pier 0, which will be built near Pier 1 of the port. The terminal will also have a metering and custody transfer station and a gas pipeline to transport the natural gas to the adjacent thermal power plants.
The LNG will be received directly between the supplying LNG carriers and the floating unit, in a configuration known as side by side, in which the vessels are moored alongside each other. The system will be able to transfer up to 6.000m³/h of LNG, through six cryogenic hoses dedicated to the transfer of the liquid fuel.
After regasification, the gas will be sent under pressure to the pipeline system through two loading arms, one main and one backup. The transfer infrastructure will have a capacity of up to 14 million m³/d, with an operating pressure of up to 100 bar.
The project provides for the construction of a carbon steel pipeline with a nominal diameter of 20 inches to connect the terminal to the existing gas pipeline network in the port area. ANP’s technical document estimates the length of this section at approximately 300m, which will have a flow capacity of up to 14 million m³/d.
The existing infrastructure must be reactivated, through a new request for an operating authorization from the ANP, to allow the transport of gas to the area designated for the thermoelectric power plants.
The terminal may operate with two regasification systems. The preferred configuration uses seawater as a heat source to vaporize the LNG. If there are environmental restrictions related to the temperature of the water returned to the sea, a closed-loop system may be adopted, in which the heat will be supplied by steam generated by burning natural gas.
In addition to the maritime structures and transfer equipment, the project will include support facilities, including an electrical substation, emergency generator, nitrogen generation plant, fire-fighting system, and control room.
In the same LRCAP, Eneva also had new thermal power plants contracted in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, which may require the construction of new LNG terminals, and in Sergipe, where it already operates a terminal.

articles.title: POSCO, Anson Advance US Lithium Project with DLE Plant Targeting 2027 - ChemAnalyst
articles.summary: POSCO, Anson Advance US Lithium Project with DLE Plant Targeting 2027  ChemAnalyst
articles.full_text:
Welcome To ChemAnalyst
	Anson Resources and POSCO Holdings have advanced plans to develop a direct lithium extraction (DLE) demonstration facility at the Green River lithium project in Utah, US, marking a key step toward validating lithium recovery technology and supporting the project's future commercial development.
	The boards of both companies have approved the terms of a binding agreement for the proposed facility, which will test POSCO Holdings' proprietary DLE technology using brines from the Green River project. The demonstration plant is designed to operate continuously at an industrial scale, providing technical data to assess the technology's performance under site-specific conditions.
	The facility will be noncommercial and will primarily focus on demonstrating the effectiveness of the extraction process rather than producing lithium for market supply. The results are expected to support Anson Resources' broader development strategy for Green River, which is being advanced as a DLE-based operation with a planned lithium carbonate production capacity of 10,000 tonnes per year.
	Under the proposed arrangement, POSCO Holdings will lead the design, construction, operation and maintenance of the demonstration plant through its proprietary technology platform. POSCO will bear the associated costs, limiting Anson Resources' direct financial exposure to the demonstration facility. In addition, POSCO will pay Anson a facilitation fee of approximately A$7.2 million, equivalent to around US$5.2 million.
	The definitive agreement was expected to be signed before the end of the second quarter of 2026. POSCO is expected to begin operating the demonstration plant in 2027, with the work scheduled for completion in 2028. The agreement is set to remain in effect until December 2028.
	The demonstration phase will be important in determining whether POSCO's extraction technology can efficiently recover lithium from Green River's brines under continuous operating conditions. Successful results could help reduce technical uncertainty, support engineering decisions and strengthen the project's prospects for future commercial development. However, the demonstration facility itself is not expected to contribute significant commercial lithium volumes.
	The planned commercial-scale project targets annual production of 10,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate, a key raw material used in lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. The project could eventually contribute to US efforts to develop domestic lithium supply chains and reduce reliance on imported battery materials.
	No specific job creation estimates, capital expenditure figures for the wider project, net present value or internal rate of return have been disclosed for the demonstration facility. Its eventual commercial impact will depend on technical results, project financing, permitting and subsequent development decisions.
	Product and Chemical Commodity Price Impact
	The demonstration facility could strengthen the long-term outlook for lithium carbonate by advancing a potential US-based supply source targeting 10,000 tonnes annually. If the technology proves commercially viable, it could improve lithium recovery efficiency and support future battery-material production. However, the noncommercial plant will not immediately increase market supply, so a direct near-term price impact is unlikely. Lithium carbonate prices will continue to depend on global electric vehicle demand, battery manufacturing activity, Chinese production, inventories and new project commissioning. Other ChemAnalyst-tracked commodities, including cobalt, nickel and graphite, are unlikely to experience material direct price changes from this development alone.

Welcome To ChemAnalyst
	Australia’s PLS Group has approved a A$1.9 billion ($1.31 billion) expansion of its flagship Pilgangoora lithium operation in Western Australia, targeting a substantial increase in spodumene concentrate production from 2029. The investment underscores the company’s confidence in long-term electric vehicle (EV) adoption and battery storage demand despite ongoing volatility in global lithium prices.
	The proposed P2000 expansion will increase Pilgangoora’s spodumene concentrate production capacity to nearly 2 million tonnes per annum (mtpa), supported by the construction of a new Jimmagunya processing plant. PLS, formerly known as Pilbara Minerals, expects the project to strengthen its competitive position in the global lithium market as battery manufacturers and automakers continue securing supplies of critical raw materials.
	The announcement also received a positive response from investors, with PLS shares climbing more than 6% in early trading, putting the stock on track for its strongest daily performance since August 24.
	A key factor behind the expansion is the application of improved processing technologies that will enable approximately 67 million tonnes of material previously classified as waste to be incorporated into the mine plan. According to the company, this development will increase Pilgangoora’s ore reserves by 23% and its contained lithium resources by 31%, improving the potential value extracted from the existing mining operation.
	PLS expects the expanded operation to deliver average annual production of approximately 1.97 million tonnes of spodumene concentrate during the first 10 years of steady-state operations. Average unit operating costs are projected to decline to around A$620 per tonne, enhancing cost competitiveness and providing greater resilience during periods of weaker lithium prices.
	Chief Executive Officer Dale Henderson said the expansion would strengthen Pilgangoora’s position on the global lithium cost curve and increase the company’s exposure to a potential recovery in lithium prices. Growing investment in electric mobility, renewable energy integration and battery energy storage continues to underpin the long-term outlook for lithium consumption.
	Beyond the core processing investment, PLS plans to spend an additional A$600 million to A$650 million on supporting infrastructure. The expenditure will cover a new accommodation village, road improvements and maintenance facilities to support the expanded operation.
	The company intends to finance the development through its A$2.3 billion cash balance and operating cash flows. It has also revised its fiscal 2027 capital expenditure forecast to between A$1.11 billion and A$1.18 billion to account for the P2000 project and associated infrastructure spending.
	The expansion will additionally generate tantalum as a by-product. The critical mineral is widely used in electronics and defence applications, offering PLS another potential revenue stream while strengthening its contribution to global critical-mineral supply chains.
	Product and Chemical Commodity Price Impact
PLS’s expansion is expected to strengthen long-term lithium supply, with higher spodumene concentrate output from 2029 potentially easing raw material constraints for lithium chemical producers. Greater concentrate availability could moderate feedstock costs for lithium carbonate and lithium hydroxide manufacturers, particularly if demand growth fails to absorb the additional supply. However, the impact will depend on EV sales, battery storage deployment, Chinese conversion capacity, inventories and competing mine closures. In the near term, construction spending is unlikely to materially alter prices. Tantalum by-product production may also improve supply availability for electronics applications, although its market impact will depend on recoverable volumes and demand.

Rather than operating commercial milling infrastructure or extracting active commercial ores, the enterprise creates shareholder value through advanced borehole geophysics, airborne electromagnetic surveys, structural core logging, and multi-rig diamond core drilling. The overarching base and precious metals backdrop presents persistent structural challenges alongside secular energy transition tailwinds. Market participants continue to differentiate sharply between established, cash-flowing senior mining producers and early-stage exploration assets whose commercial potential lies in distant operating cycles.

- Geopolitical tensions: Persistent international friction, including Middle East conflicts involving the United States and Iran, creates systemic volatility across global energy benchmarks, trade corridors, and financial markets. secure and clean energy supply is also driving demand for new nuclear power and
uranium is the key beneficiary of that growth."
Industrial
Info Resources is tracking 101
uranium mining projects in the U.S. with a total investment value (TIV) of
$8.62 billion. The project count is up by eight since July, signifying the
sector's continued growth.
Nuclear
power growth includes both restarts of retired plants and additions involving
newer nuclear technologies including small modular reactors (SMRs).
Will High Prices Affect Electricity Costs or Plant Planning?
As fuel
accounts for only 1-2% of nuclear power plant costs, higher uranium costs are
not expected to noticeably affect grid pricing or the planning/completion of
new reactor construction.
Production Growth Has a Long Way to Go
Uranium
prices have risen in spite of an increase in domestic mining. For more
information, see July 15, 2026, article - U.S.
Domestic Uranium Mining Grows to Supply Energy Security and the SMR Future.
The U.S.
Energy Information Administration (EIA) said that 2025's triuranium octoxide
(U3O8), or uranium concentrate, at 2.1 million pounds, was more than triple
that of 2024's total. U3O8 is the precursor to a multi-step process that leads
to low-enriched uranium (LEU) and other end-use uranium levels.
While that
sounds significant, even at the higher amounts the U.S. accounts for only about
1% of world uranium mining, and it imports 99% of what it uses, according to
2023 EIA figures. Most imports come from three nations: Canada, Australia and
Kazakhstan.
Nuclear Power Demand Also on Upswing
Industrial
Info Resources has reported that nuclear power, especially from SMRs, has
suddenly become an "all-hands-on-deck" situation. Data-center growth is
certainly a key, but so is the rising adoption of EVs and the electrification
of industry. For more on that, see July 24, 2026, article - Nuclear
Resurgence Spurs Permitting, Supply Chain Issues.
Industrial Info Resources is tracking 54 SMR
capital-spending projects in the U.S., with a total investment value (TIV) of
nearly $160 billion. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on
these developments in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Project
Database, where readers can find details--including construction schedules,
investment values and necessary equipment--in a detailed list of project reports."
Mining, then Refining
Energy
security being a high priority, the U.S. has invested heavily in both mining
and in processing, both of which must be done domestically to secure the
supply. The EIA stated that 2025's U.S. in-situ recovery (ISR) capacity was
13.3 million pounds, accounting for just over a third of the 32 million pounds
it uses each year. That was actually a slight decrease from the 14.1 million
pounds capacity of 2024.
That number
could be headed back up, as five ISR plants were on standby as of the end of
2025 with a combined annual production capacity of 8.8 million pounds U3O8.
More, More, More
With the
twin issues of rising demand and the domestic sourcing of energy supplies in
order reduce international uncertainty, many see the future for all phases of
the nuclear industry, from ore to electrons, as having significant growth
potential.
