articles.title: Chemical engineers say hydrogen is ‘essential’ to the future power mix at IChemE conference - The Chemical Engineer
articles.summary: Chemical engineers say hydrogen is ‘essential’ to the future power mix at IChemE conference  The Chemical Engineer
articles.full_text:
Hydrogen is an inextricable component in decarbonising the world’s energy systems. But despite its varied uses case for power and heavy industries, it does not come without trade-offs in cost and technical readiness.
More than a hundred academic and industry leaders confronted the complexities of hydrogen at IChemE’s new Hydrogen Innovation and Technology Conference in Manchester.
Engineering professionals from the likes of ExxonMobil, Johnson Matthey, WSP and the UK government delivered around 40 presentations covering the investment needs of the hydrogen industry, current innovations in generation and transportation, and the policies and standards that must be implemented to secure a solid foundation for hydrogen demand to thrive.
Joan Cordiner, co-chair of the conference and president elect of IChemE, said: “There has been a lot of debate about hydrogen and where it fits in our world. I want to foster good discussions on the reality of this resource. As chemical engineers, the one thing we know we are good at is solving problems, so please ask questions, even if they seem stupid – those are the questions which push innovation.”
One of hydrogen’s major bottlenecks is in its applications, particularly in which areas of decarbonisation it could create the most value. With ambitions of domestic heating and chemical feedstock very much in trials around the world, and with much progress in Scandinavia with the NORHyWAY hydrogen valley, the most interest has been found with heavy industry.
Paul Henderson, who leads the UK government’s strategic approach to hydrogen, explained how there is "no one-size-fits-all” approach to the power source.
"The overarching principle we are working with is electrification first as the most low-cost solution for decarbonisation, and for everything after that, specifically in heavy industry, hydrogen is part of the solution.”
The UK's new Andy Burnham-led government, which is focused on bringing down energy costs for consumers, has yet to release a dedicated hydrogen strategy to follow up the 2021 report. However, Henderson says the government is very much working with industry to develop strong policies and resources around the understanding and implementation of hydrogen in the UK. He gave an update to the conference on the government's first Hydrogen Allocation Round (HAR1), which has several projects that have now reached final investment decisions.
Government support is essential for industry to progress with hydrogen projects and innovation, as ambiguity around regulation and funding can hinder, and even cancel delivery. Earlier this year, Scottish Energy firm SSE decided to pause several ambitious hydrogen projects, including its blue hydrogenH2NorthEast project in Teesside, due to policy delays and a lack of project support in the UK.
Emma Guthrie, the CEO of the Hydrogen Energy Association, said: "As we go through decarbonisation, we do need to consider the role of molecules like hydrogen, as well as electrons."
She added: "Though the ball is starting to roll again now, industry does struggle when the government is inconsistent."
Cost was an unavoidable conversation at the conference. Hydrogen of all colours, including renewable-backed green hydrogen to natural-gas powered grey hydrogen, all come with their varying funding needs, as with developing new technologies, investment is needed for new equipment, modifications, pipelines, and transportation.
Another setback for investment comes with the safety of hydrogen. As hydrogen is a much smaller and lighter molecule compared to gas, there is a risk of it escaping when in storage or when moving through pipelines. This risk is a worry for investors, who must ultimately have to manage the risk and take a chance on the technology for demand to grow.
Elizaveta Kovaleva from Oxera Consulting LLP, discussed what private investors need when investing in hydrogen, and why many can be reluctant.
"Investors need a balance of risk and return. They need to know what cash flow they will get and the risk affecting it. And this includes volume risk, construction risk, regulatory and political risk, and operating risk."
She adds: "Investors need a balance of risk and return, and with where hydrogen is at the moment, there should be more focus on de-risking hydrogen to attract investors."
Despite this skepticism, chemical engineers have been working to build safe and efficient processes for handling hydrogen which are both financially feasible and scalable.
Gemma Simpson, the live trial operations manager for the LTS Futures project from gas distributor SGN, shared the lessons learned from the scheme, based in Grangemouth, and how it has built a "blueprint" for companies looking to safely and efficiently utilise existing gas pipelines for hydrogen transportation and generation.
Through rigorous pipeline and workforce testing and training, the plan showed that hydrogen could be transported safely, and has developed a set of parameters operators must take into account when it comes to modifications and selecting the most effective pipelines for hydrogen.
In parallel, Rob Crane, technology, scouting and venturing manager at ExxonMobil, and director of the American Institute of Chemical Engineers (AIChE), discussed Exxon's development of methane pyrolysis-produced hydrogen, and its scale opportunities.
For legacy oil and gas firms like ExxonMobil, methane pyrolysis is a competitive route to hydrogen production, as the company has decades of expertise in hydrocarbons, and they will know how to further process the byproduct of solid carbon. ExxonMobil has a sharp scaleup plan for methane pyrolysis hydrogen, already running a pilot plant in Ludwigshafen, Germany, with BASF, which produces around 10 t/y of hydrogen and 30 t/y of carbon.
With various cases made for different types of hydrogen production and its circulation, all attendees agreed that it was needed for global decarbonisation.
Ollie Folayan, president of the IChemE, said that the hydrogen industry could not grow without the expertise of chemical engineers, who know the industry better than other experts as it is based in learned principles and systems thinking.
"The last 6 years working in the hydrogen sector have been the most enjoyable of my career as I have worked on projects which I never have experienced before, but I know exactly how to do. With hydrogen, you are working with old technologies and applying them to new situations."

P2X Solutions is injecting renewable e-methane produced at its plant in Finland into the country’s natural gas network, enabling distribution to domestic customers and access to other European markets via the Balticconnector pipeline. Gasgrid, Finland’s state-owned gas transmission system operator, has issued the country’s first guarantees of origin for renewable e-methane produced at the facility. The certificates enable the renewable origin of the synthetic methane to be documented and verified, allowing customers to distinguish it from fossil natural gas. E-methane is produced by combining renewable hydrogen with captured carbon dioxide, creating a synthetic gas that can be transported and used through existing natural gas infrastructure. “Gasgrid has been issuing guarantees of origin for biomethane for almost five years and for hydrogen for around a year,” said the Finnish company. The issuance of the first e-methane certificates marks a further step in Finland’s efforts to integrate renewable gases into its energy system and facilitate their trade across European markets.tself.
Stargate Hydrogen launched a proprietary ceramic catalyst that reportedly increases the output efficiency of its alkaline electrolysers stacks to 48 kWh/kg while eliminating all dependency on iridium and other platinum-group metals (PGMs). The product is available in stacks up to 0.5 MW, with integration into the 5 MW stack underway. “Stargate Hydrogen’s factory currently produces 140 MW annually, with capacity expandable to 1 GW+ through incremental investment,” said the Estonia-based company.
ITM Power announced that its build-own-operate (BOO) subsidiary, Hydropulse, has signed Heads of Terms with a European oil refinery for a large-scale green hydrogen project. “The project in development comprises 150 MW of ITM Power’s Alpha electrolyser platform to produce green hydrogen on site under a 10-year agreement,” said the UK-based company. The parties are targeting Final Investment Decision (FID) in 2027, with hydrogen production expected to commence in 2029.
STX Group announced its first offtake of Renewable Fuel of Non-Biological Origin (Rfbno)-compliant e-methane, produced by Turn2X at its first commercial plant in Spain. “The first delivery of fully Rfnbo certified e-methane took place early in October 2026. The companies are also in active discussions to work together on future commercial-scale e-methane projects,” explained the Amsterdam-headquartered commodity trader.
Nel and Rheinmetall AG have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to explore joint opportunities in decentralised renewable fuel production. “The collaboration will combine Nel’s electrolyser technology with Rheinmetall’s Giga PtX concept and systems-integration expertise to assess scalable, modular solutions for the localised production of low-carbon synthetic fuels for defence and critical infrastructure applications”, said the Norwegian company. The Oslo-based company has also received a purchase order from an undisclosed US-based technology company for multiple containerized PEM electrolyser units, the MC-series, and related services, with a total value of about $12 million, said the Norwegian company, adding that the estimated delivery is in 2027. Nel’s MC-series is a containerized PEM electrolyser platform designed for scalable, reliable and efficient on-site hydrogen production.
Jera has invested in Koloma, a US-based natural hydrogen exploration and development company. Headquartered in Denver, Colorado, Koloma combines proprietary geological data, specialized exploration tools and field experience to identify and evaluate prospective natural hydrogen resources. The company has raised more than $400 million from investors including Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Khosla Ventures and Amazon, said the Japanese company.
Hy24 has signed an agreement with EDF’s venture capital arm to acquire Hynamics, a subsidiary of the EDF Group. The transaction could be completed in the first quarter of 2027, said the French asset manager and the world’s largest investment platform dedicated to low-carbon hydrogen. Hynamics produces and markets low-carbon hydrogen for the heavy mobility and industrial sectors through projects in France and the United Kingdom. “This transaction marks a new stage in Hynamics’ development, with the ambition of fostering the creation of a leading French and British low-carbon hydrogen champion,” said EDF.

Venture Global, Inc. has entered into power and grid frame agreements with GE Vernova and Baker Hughes Energy Services for up to 16 new, 720 MW power island units and associated power transformer equipment, supporting the continued expansion of its existing behind-the-meter, Island-Mode industrial power network that is not reliant on the grid.
The agreements will enable continued growth in Venture Global’s LNG business and provide a pathway to make up to 10 GW of new compute capacity available over time – at sites owned or controlled by the company – for potential adjacent infrastructure and data centres. With Island Mode power generated using this incremental dedicated on-site infrastructure, the expansion would place no additional demand on the public electric grid or public water utilities and, therefore, have no added costs to local consumers. This new capacity would build on the company’s 4.5 GW of Island Mode modular, gas-fired generation that has and will continue to supply power to our facilities.
“Over the last decade, Venture Global has successfully built complex energy infrastructure, including one of the world’s largest private industrial electric grids that supports our core LNG export business. Our power generation platform is not reliant on the grid and reliably runs completely behind-the-meter making this new opportunity a natural extension of what we are experienced and proven to do safely, reliably, and at-scale,” said Venture Global CEO, Mike Sabel.
“These new agreements outline a phased, disciplined expansion to make reliable, large scale power capacity available for new compute as and when we elect. By providing Island-Mode power generation, gas supply, closed-loop water systems, thousands of acres of land, data centres, and other necessary infrastructure, Venture Global is creating a vertically integrated AI utility that could solve for the many chokepoints associated with the AI buildout. This advances Venture Global’s broader strategy of strengthening America’s critical energy infrastructure and addressing one of the most important infrastructure challenges facing our nation today.”
The agreements provide that the company may enter into certain definitive reservation agreements, which contain agreed pricing and delivery terms, to reserve manufacturing capability over time. This framework preserves Venture Global’s flexibility on the timing and scope of future deployments. Venture Global currently expects to place its first power island purchase order by the end of 2026.
The 720 MW power island units would consist of combined cycle gas turbines and certain related equipment, utilising configurations consistent with Venture Global’s existing power infrastructure.
